clue.text: Fun clothes.?

parts.note: the costume worn for fun is the chequered outfit of a court jester

explanation.surface: A question about what to wear to a fancy-dress party.
explanation.definitionFit: Motley was the parti-coloured costume of the professional fool, so it is literally clothing for fun-making.

clue.text: Fellow at the board on board

definitions.text: Fellow at the board on board

parts.words: Fellow at the board on board
parts.note: a board is a dining table, and on board a ship sailors eat together in groups

explanation.surface: A fellow company director sitting at the boardroom table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Board' first means a table for meals, then a ship's deck: a shipmate who eats at the same table.
explanation.definitionFit: A sailor who shares the same mess, or eating group, aboard ship is this companion.

clue.text: How is Janus looking ?

parts.note: the Roman god Janus has two heads looking opposite ways

explanation.surface: Someone asks after the appearance of the Roman god of doorways.
explanation.walkthrough: Janus is shown with one face looking forward and one back, and the word for that also means deceitful.
explanation.definitionFit: Janus literally has a pair of faces, and the word figuratively means hypocritical.

clue.text: Do I cause trouble, being a glutton ?

indicators.note: to trouble something is to stir it up, so the letters are disturbed into a new order

explanation.surface: A guilty eater wonders whether greed makes them a nuisance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trouble' turns the letters of 'Do I cause' into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means voracious or greedy, the quality of someone who overeats.

clue.text: Cyclist intent on getting a tan?

definitions.text: Cyclist intent on getting a tan?

parts.words: Cyclist intent on getting a tan?
parts.note: an old slang word for a reckless speeding cyclist is also a word for a blazing hot day, the kind that tans you

explanation.surface: A sun-worshipping cyclist pedals hard in summer.
explanation.walkthrough: The feed reads 'can'; the page prints 'tan'. The answer is old slang for a cyclist who rides furiously fast, and also a very hot day, when a tan is got.
explanation.definitionFit: A fast reckless rider was called this in the 1890s, and a sweltering summer day carries the same name.

clue.text: Mountebanks

parts.note: travelling sellers of quack remedies, a byword for frauds and impostors

explanation.definitionFit: Both words name swindlers who claim skills they lack, like quack-medicine sellers.

clue.text: The gentle addressee ?

parts.note: authors of old often spoke to the person holding the book as 'gentle' followed by a title

explanation.surface: A polite person to whom a letter is sent.
explanation.walkthrough: Old authors addressed 'gentle reader', the person turning the pages.
explanation.definitionFit: An author speaking in print addresses whoever is reading the book.

clue.text: Draw on the manuscript-of Stalky and Co. perhaps!

parts.note: to draw a load is to pull or haul it

explanation.surface: A writer draws on Kipling's school-story manuscript.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stalky and Co.' is Kipling's book, but here it means stalks and company: the stems of potatoes or beans.
explanation.definitionFit: These are the stems or stalks of crops such as peas, beans and potatoes.

clue.text: Spreading light by agreement in endless Wagner

indicators.note: the word for agreement goes inside the word for Wagner's cycle

parts.note: Wagner's opera cycle is The Ring, and a ring is a thing with no end
ay or aye is an old word of agreement, meaning yes

explanation.surface: Light spreads by consent through an interminable Wagner opera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless' looks like an instruction to drop a last letter; it describes a ring, which has no end, so 'endless Wagner' is his Ring cycle.
explanation.definitionFit: To ray is to send out beams, so the participle means emitting light.

clue.text: As long as one can get on the banner

indicators.note: the letters of the opening words are what one can get from them by rearranging them

explanation.surface: Protesters want their message to stay on the banner for as long as possible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As long as one can get' reads like a time phrase; it says the letters of 'As long' can be rearranged to give the answer, the words on the banner.
explanation.definitionFit: A catchphrase or motto is what protesters paint on a banner.

clue.text: Where to get a nice cup of yerba mate

definitions.text: Where to get a nice cup of yerba mate

parts.words: Where to get a nice cup of yerba mate
parts.note: yerba mate is a holly-leaf tea drunk across South America, especially in one landlocked country

explanation.surface: A traveller asks where the best herbal tea is served.
explanation.walkthrough: Yerba mate, also called Paraguay tea, is the national drink of this South American country.
explanation.definitionFit: The tea is so tied to the country that it is often sold as Paraguay tea.

clue.text: Do you tell me a lie, Maizie ?

explanation.surface: Someone challenges a girl called Maizie to tell a fib.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maizie' looks like a girl's name; it stands for maize, as in 'maize-y'. The answer is South African for maize, spelt by the three words 'me a lie' run together.
explanation.definitionFit: In South Africa an ear of maize, or maize itself, is called by this word.

clue.text: The old boy's up at the Town Hall

definitions.text: The old boy's up at the Town Hall

parts.words: The old boy's up at the Town Hall
parts.note: an old boy is an older man, and a senior council member works at the town hall; the title even sounds like 'older man'

explanation.surface: Grandad has gone up to the council offices.
explanation.definitionFit: A senior member of a borough council, historically an elder, sits in the town hall.

clue.text: Lipstick by Herrick ?

parts.note: Robert Herrick wrote a poem comparing a girl's lips to fruit ready for picking, and its title is a cosmetic shade

explanation.surface: A cosmetics brand named after a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Herrick's poem 'Cherry-Ripe' praises red lips; the name was also used for a lipstick shade.
explanation.definitionFit: The title of Herrick's poem about red lips suits a red lipstick.

clue.text: Mixed-up cherub in complicated test for missile-projectors

indicators.note: one rearranged word is placed inside the other rearranged word
something complicated is tangled, so the letters of test are jumbled
mixed-up letters of cherub are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A confused angel sits a hard exam on siege weapons.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged cherub sits inside the rearranged test, which splits round it as T at the front and three letters at the back; 'for' links wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: These were medieval siege engines that hurled stones by a counterweighted arm.

clue.text: Poe evidently admired Helen's mauve rinse!

definitions.text: Poe evidently admired Helen's mauve rinse!

parts.words: Poe evidently admired Helen's mauve rinse!
parts.note: Poe's poem 'To Helen' praises her flower-coloured hair, read here as a dyed tint

explanation.surface: A poet appreciated a woman's tinted hairdo.
explanation.walkthrough: Poe's 'To Helen' speaks of her 'hyacinth hair'; the clue pretends this was a purple hair rinse.
explanation.definitionFit: The flower named in Poe's line is often mauve or purple, the shade of the rinse.

clue.text: Silently takes in in great detail

indicators.note: the word for silently takes the next word inside itself

parts.note: to act silently is to act mutely

explanation.surface: Someone quietly absorbs every particular.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue has two copies of 'in': the first is the word taken inside, the second opens the definition, so nothing is used twice.
explanation.definitionFit: Examining something in very small particulars means examining it closely and precisely.

clue.text: Mrs. Weaver? The night was her undoing

definitions.text: Mrs. Weaver? The night was her undoing

parts.words: Mrs. Weaver? The night was her undoing
parts.note: Odysseus's wife wove a shroud by day and unpicked it by night to delay her suitors

explanation.surface: A married woman's ruin came one evening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Undoing' looks like ruin; Odysseus's wife unravelled her day's weaving every night to keep suitors waiting.
explanation.definitionFit: Ulysses's faithful wife is the weaver of Homer's Odyssey who undid her work at night.

clue.text: Intoxicating American battle

parts.note: a strong spirit made from distilled wine is an intoxicating drink
the fermented juice of grapes is another intoxicating drink

explanation.surface: A drunken fight breaks out in the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: One word 'Intoxicating' supplies two drinks, one after the other. The battle of Brandywine (1777) was fought in Pennsylvania in the American War of Independence.
explanation.definitionFit: Washington's army was defeated by the British at this creek in Pennsylvania in 1777.

clue.text: " A dust whom England bore, , made aware " (Brooke)

definitions.text: " A dust whom England bore, , made aware " (Brooke)

parts.words: " A dust whom England bore, , made aware " (Brooke)
parts.note: the gap is the missing word in Rupert Brooke's sonnet 'The Soldier'

explanation.surface: A line of a war poem with a word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Brooke's line reads 'A dust whom England bore, shaped, made aware'; the solver supplies the missing word.
explanation.definitionFit: The gap in Brooke's line is filled by the past tense of a verb meaning formed.

clue.text: Vagabonds run to them

indicators.note: the word run is joined to the answer to make vagabonds, so it is the part taken away

parts.note: runagates is an archaic word for wanderers and fugitives

explanation.surface: Tramps hurry towards some people.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue says vagabonds are 'run' added to them: RUNAGATES less RUN. 'Them' stands for the answer, the striped stones.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun points at the answer itself, the banded semi-precious stones.

clue.text: Or dare to be a lover ?

indicators.note: the letters of the words are invited to become something else by rearrangement

explanation.surface: A shy person is urged to dare to fall in love.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be' says the letters of 'Or dare' are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: One who worships or loves someone devotedly is their lover.

clue.text: How time flies on them!

parts.note: on festival days and holidays the hours pass quickly because one is enjoying oneself

explanation.surface: An exclamation about how quickly time passes.
explanation.walkthrough: The feed reads 'lies'; the page prints 'flies'. The answer is a pair of words, as in 'high days and holidays', meaning festivals.
explanation.definitionFit: Festive occasions pass quickly because they are enjoyed.

clue.text: What did Zola do in L'Aurore ?

definitions.text: What did Zola do in L'Aurore

parts.words: What did Zola do in L'Aurore
parts.note: Emile Zola's open letter in the Paris newspaper L'Aurore in 1898 was headed with a charge against the authorities

explanation.surface: A question about a French writer's newspaper article.
explanation.walkthrough: Zola's letter on the Dreyfus affair was printed in L'Aurore under the headline 'J'accuse', French for 'I charge'.
explanation.definitionFit: Zola publicly charged the army and government with covering up the Dreyfus injustice.

clue.text: Youthful skull-finder on the field of Blenheim

definitions.text: Youthful skull-finder on the field of Blenheim

parts.words: Youthful skull-finder on the field of Blenheim
parts.note: in Southey's poem 'After Blenheim' a little boy finds a skull by the stream where the battle was fought

explanation.surface: A child turns up a skull on an old battlefield.
explanation.walkthrough: In Robert Southey's poem 'After Blenheim', old Kaspar's grandson finds a skull and asks what the battle was about.
explanation.definitionFit: Little Peterkin is the boy in the poem who brings old Kaspar the skull.

clue.text: Private in Italy

parts.note: Eric Linklater's 1946 novel follows a gentle Italian soldier of the lowest rank through the war

explanation.surface: A soldier of the lowest rank serving in Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Private' is not secrecy but a rank: Linklater's novel 'Private Angelo' tells of an Italian private soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: The title character of Linklater's novel is an Italian army private named this.

clue.text: Showing Valou ?

parts.note: the proverb says discretion is the better part of valour, so showing the better part of valour means being careful

explanation.surface: A question about displaying courage.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints 'Valou', a dropped letter for 'Valour'. Falstaff's saying 'the better part of valour is discretion' makes a cautious person one who shows valour.
explanation.definitionFit: Proverbially, prudence is the better part of valour, so being circumspect is a show of it.

clue.text: A bit fettered in Chelsea ? What a row !

definitions.text: A bit fettered in Chelsea ? What a row

parts.words: A bit fettered in Chelsea ? What a row
parts.note: a street name in Chelsea sounds like a link of fetters, and is the name of a famous row of houses

explanation.surface: Someone in a smart London district is tied up, causing a fuss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' is not a quarrel but a street: Cheyne Row and Cheyne Walk are in Chelsea, a London district, and the name sounds like 'chain'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheyne Row is a Chelsea street where Thomas Carlyle lived, and its name is said like a fetter's chain.
